newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Growers say rain needed in key Brazil soybean area.
newsitem.headline: Growers say rain needed in key Brazil soybean area.

text.p: Growers in the key Brazilian soybean growing region of Rio Grande do Sul said soil moisture was getting low and they needed fresh rains within a week to avoid any significant crop losses.
"We need rain here, we already have some small losses," said Joao Henrich, agronomist at the Cotriba cooperative in Ibiruba.

Some regions have not had any rain for two weeks and the lack of moisture was affecting mainly soybeans in the grain formation stage, agronomists said. The harvest is due to begin at the end of this month in the state.
"We have 20 percent of the harvest ready to be harvested and 70 percent in the grain formation stage," Henrich said, but he added that current losses were too small to quantify.

There was a prospect for scattered showers on March 20, but the next three to four days would be sunny with little chance of rain, according to the National Institute of Meteorology. No cold front was seen heading for the region at present, it said.
"We need at least 50 mm of rain for the situation to normalise, as soon as possible," Henrich said.

Zigomar Carra at the Cotrisana cooperative in Sananduva said the region needed 60 to 70 mm of rain for soil moisture to be at a comfortable level. He estimated his region already had a crop loss of five percent due to the dry weather.
But most agronomists said the situation was not yet critical and crop losses were minimal.
"The crop is already beginning to feel the lack of moisture," said Flavio Nai, agronomist at the Coorondinha cooperative in Rondinha.
But he added, "For soybeans, losses are still small at around two percent. We are having much more trouble with diseases."
Meanwhile, in Parana the weather was favourable to the continuation of the harvest.
"Parana already has 50 percent of its crop harvested and will harvest another 30 percent in the next 10 days," said Nelson Costa at the Parana cooperatives association Ocepar.
"We are having no problem with dry weather at all, if anything there is the prospect that rain will delay the harvest in some areas," he added.
